overview:
On 20 March 2003 a coalition led by the United States and Britain invaded Iraq, arguing that Saddam Hussein retained weapons of mass destruction and defied UN disarmament demands. The conventional campaign was brief: armored columns pushed north from Kuwait, Baghdad fell in early April after a short, chaotic fight for the capital, and Saddam's statue came down in Firdos Square on 9 April. No stockpiles of banned weapons were ever found. Britain's own Chilcot inquiry concluded years later that the intelligence had been presented with unwarranted certainty, that peaceful options had not been exhausted, and that planning for what came after was wholly inadequate. Two decisions by the occupying Coalition Provisional Authority in May 2003 — purging Baath Party members from public life and dissolving the Iraqi army — turned hundreds of thousands of armed, trained men into unemployed opponents of the occupation almost overnight.

An insurgency took shape within months, and the war's remaining eight years were fought in cities rather than deserts. Fallujah was stormed twice in 2004, the second assault in November being the heaviest urban combat American troops had seen since Vietnam; Najaf saw fighting with Moqtada al-Sadr's Mahdi Army the same summer; Tal Afar, Ramadi and other towns along the Euphrates and the Syrian border were cleared and re-cleared. Saddam himself was pulled from a hole near Tikrit in December 2003 and hanged three years later. But the deadliest phase was not the fight against the occupier. After the bombing of the Shia shrine at Samarra in February 2006, Sunni and Shia militias fell into sectarian killing that emptied whole neighborhoods of Baghdad and displaced millions. A US troop "surge" in 2007, paired with Sunni tribal groups turning against al-Qaeda in Iraq, brought violence down from its peak; the same year, Blackwater contractors killed seventeen civilians in Nisour Square, a case that came to stand for the impunity of the occupation's private armies. Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki's government moved against the Sadrists in Basra in 2008, and a status-of-forces agreement set the clock for departure. The last American combat troops left in December 2011.

Counting the dead has itself been contested. Iraq Body Count documented roughly 114,000 civilian deaths from violence across 2003–2011 from press and official records, while acknowledging the real figure must be higher; household survey estimates run several times that, one widely cited study putting war-attributable deaths near half a million. Around 4,500 American service members died, alongside coalition troops, contractors, and Iraqi soldiers and police whose losses were never systematically recorded.
significance: The war reshaped the region it was meant to stabilize. It removed the main Sunni Arab counterweight to Iran and left Tehran with deep influence in Baghdad; it wrecked Iraq's institutions and hardened a sectarian logic in its politics; and the insurgent networks it fostered, driven underground by 2011, re-emerged as the Islamic State and seized a third of the country in 2014. Elsewhere it burned through the international goodwill the United States held after September 2001, made "weapons of mass destruction" a byword for intelligence bent to a policy decision already taken, and left publics in both invading countries far more skeptical of the case for future wars — a caution visible in Western hesitancy over Syria and beyond. Its unresolved legal question, whether the invasion was lawful without an explicit Security Council authorization, still shadows arguments about when states may use force.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia and Britannica overviews, Iraq Body Count's 2003–2011 tally, the Brown University Costs of War project, and the Chilcot inquiry's executive summary. The dataset's 23 events skew heavily toward set-piece battles and named US operations, mostly 2003–2008, so the invasion and the counterinsurgency are well represented while the sectarian civil war of 2006–07, Abu Ghraib, the elections and constitutional fights, the Anbar Awakening, and the mass-casualty bombings that killed most civilians are thin or absent. The wider record is lopsided in the same direction: American and British military and government sources are voluminous and largely declassified, while Iraqi civilian deaths were never officially counted, insurgent groups left almost no usable archive, and survey-based mortality estimates diverge by a factor of four or more.
